https://www.newsandstar.co.uk/news/26409.text: Business People Carlisle New market stall serving up Hungarian food in Carlisle By Matthew Graham Reporter Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A NEW market stall is serving up European flavours with a twist. Nokedli, a Hungarian street food stall, is now open inside Carlisle 's Market Hall serving up homemade Hungarian pasta and customisable salads and fries. Father-daughter team Laszlo (Les) and Szilvia Varga, who run the family-owned business, chose the location for its central location. More choices for customers (Image: Supplied) Szilvia Varga said: "Since moving to Carlisle eight years ago, the Market Hall has always been one of our favorite places for food. "It’s such a central and historical hub for the city and with recent renovations it’s only become a greater asset. "So when looking for a venue, it really was a ‘why not here’? question than a ‘why should we?’ question." The pair serve up nokedli, a Hungarian noodle dish that is lighter than traditional pasta and can be paired with a choice of sauces and toppings. Flavours include tomato, cheese, garlic mushroom, and butter and herb, with protein options such as chicken, steak, halloumi, or mushrooms. Customers can build their own bowl or choose from a set menu, with new specials featured weekly. For those looking for something different, noodles aren't the only option on the menu. They also serve customisable salads and fries, and drinks from a selection of canned drinks. They are currently exploring the addition of a coffee machine. Szilvia said: "The different flavours and opportunity to customise. "Nokedli is a versatile meal that can be mixed with different sauces and toppings. "So you can always have something new." The stall is open from Tuesday to Saturday, 11am to 3pm. Some of the dishes on offer (Image: Supplied) All dishes are served in takeaway bowls, and lids are available for those who want to enjoy their meal elsewhere. The team have plans to expand the menu and introduce offers in the coming months. Szilvia said: "We definitely have a few ideas brewing in our pot. "We have our weekly specials and will be hosting online polls to see what people are most interested in. "The specials range from traditional Hungarian dishes (like lángos) to other cuisines, like chili con carne. "We are also looking into meal-deal offers, such as adding side salads with your main meal. "Desserts may also be in the works." The business encourages customers to follow updates and specials through social media or by stopping by the stall in person. http://global.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202608.text: China Edition ASIA 中文 HOME OPINION VIDEO WORLD TECH CHINA BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL SPORTS HOME OPINION VIDEO WORLD CHINA TECHNOLOGY BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL SPORTS SERVICE NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper Subscribe Meta to pay $18b to settle states' teen safety lawsuit Updated: 2026-08-28 09:25 OAKLAND — Meta has agreed to pay up to $18 billion over a decade and impose sweeping new restrictions on how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram under a settlement with nearly all US states over allegations that the company designed its platforms to hook young users. The main settlement, approved by a federal judge, resolves claims by 29 states that Meta engineered its platforms to hook children, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13. Texas reached a separate agreement with Meta, bringing the total potential payout to about $18 billion. Meta agreed to automatically block teenagers from accessing Facebook and Instagram between midnight and 6 am local time without parental consent. Teenage accounts will also be capped by default at two hours of cumulative daily use across Meta's apps, although time spent messaging or watching long-form video will not count toward the limit. Meta said the agreement could serve as a template for the wider industry and called on competitors, including TikTok and YouTube, to adopt similar measures. If competing platforms make equivalent commitments, the overnight lockout would last from 10 pm to 7 am, while the daily allowance would fall to 60 minutes per app, capped at two hours in total. An independent auditor jointly chosen by Meta and the states and paid for by the company will monitor compliance for 10 years. The settlement will also require Meta to strengthen age verification and disable certain features for teens that could encourage excessive use. Allegations denied The agreement does not constitute an admission of liability or wrongdoing by Meta, which has consistently denied the allegations. It ends the trial in its second week, after testimony from Instagram head Adam Mosseri and other witnesses about the effectiveness of the company's teen safety measures. The settlement comes as governments worldwide step up efforts to limit children's exposure to social media risks. The European Commission said it expected Meta to address the "addictive design" of its platforms in Europe and offer similar commitments to protect children in the EU. Australia, which introduced a minimum age of 16 for social media late last year, said the agreement showed that platforms have tools to better protect young users. Poland's Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski asked the European Commission to fine Meta 250 million euros ($291 million), citing inadequate controls over fraudulent advertisements. Meta said it was investing in technologies and partnerships with industry and law enforcement to find and remove scammers. https://prague.tv/prague-now/paying-in-p.text: Need to know Where Prague and the rest of Czechia When Cards are accepted at most hours; some small places are cash only The short version Czechia uses the Czech crown (CZK), not the euro. Contactless cards and phones work in most shops, restaurants and cafés. Always choose to pay in CZK if a terminal or ATM offers your home currency. Keep a little cash for small pubs, market stalls, public toilets and tipping. On this page 11 sections Do I need Czech crowns? Are cards widely accepted? Can I pay for public transport by card? What about tipping? Where should I get cash? What is dynamic currency conversion? What should I carry? A day of paying, in order Is it safe to use my card in Prague? What if I run out of cash on a Sunday? Small things You tap your phone for a flat white, tap again for a tram ticket, and feel thoroughly modern. Then you reach a station toilet, or a sausage stand, and the only thing that works is a coin. Prague is nearly cashless, and the exceptions are what catch people out. The answers below cover what is accepted where, how to get cash without being fleeced, and the one screen prompt that quietly costs people money. Do I need Czech crowns? Yes, a few. Czechia is in the EU but not the eurozone, so the currency is the Czech crown ( koruna , written CZK or Kč). Some tourist shops will take euros, but they give you a poor rate and hand back change in crowns. Crowns, or a card, are almost always better. Are cards widely accepted? Mostly, yes. Contactless payment by card, phone or watch is normal in supermarkets, restaurants, cafés, many pubs, museums and larger shops. Small purchases rarely need a PIN, though a terminal may ask for one. It's the exceptions that catch people out. Some small pubs, market stalls, food stands and independent shops prefer cash or take nothing else. Public toilets in stations and elsewhere often want coins. Look for a card sticker on the door, or ask before you order. Card or cash? Feature Card or phone works Bring cash or coins Food Supermarkets, restaurants, cafés, many pubs Small pubs, market stalls, food stands Getting around PID app and many machines (check pid.cz) Some machines are coins only Sights Museums and larger attractions Small independent shops and some small venues Tips Possible, if you say so before the terminal comes out Easiest by far, in small notes and coins Public toilets Rarely Often coins only Acceptance varies from place to place. A card sticker on the door is the quick check. Can I pay for public transport by card? Tickets are sold through the PID app, at ticket machines and at selected points. Station machines take coins and often cards, but they differ from machine to machine. PID has changed how it handles contactless bank-card payments for fares in the past, so check pid.cz before you travel (as of 2026; check the official source). Don't board without a valid ticket. Inspectors do check. What about tipping? Tipping is customary in restaurants and pubs, usually by rounding up or adding around 10 per cent. Say the total you want to pay as you hand over the money, as described in our guide to how a Czech pub works . If you're paying by card, mention the tip before the terminal comes out, because adding it afterwards is awkward. Cash is easiest for tips, so keep some small notes and coins. Where should I get cash? An ATM attached to a bank branch is generally the safest choice. Free-standing machines on busy tourist streets can charge higher fees and offer weak exchange rates. Check the fees on screen before you confirm, and ask your own bank what it charges for foreign withdrawals. Exchange offices are everywhere and vary hugely. Compare buy and sell rates, ignore "no commission" signs and walk a few streets from the main sights (more in our guide to tourist traps and scams ). For most visitors the simplest plan is a modest withdrawal from a bank ATM on arrival, then cards for the rest. What is dynamic currency conversion? When you pay by card or withdraw cash abroad, the terminal or ATM may ask whether you want to be charged in your home currency or in CZK. Choose CZK. The home-currency option mainly suits the merchant, and the rate behind it is generally worse than your own bank's. If in doubt, press the CZK option and move on. The screen that costs you money A terminal asking 'Pay in EUR, USD or GBP?' is offering to convert the money for you, at its rate. Press CZK every time, on terminals and ATMs alike. What should I carry? A contactless card, plus a spare kept in a different place in case one is blocked or lost. A little cash in crowns: enough for a coffee, a tip, a toilet or a stall. Your phone with a wallet app, if you use one. Many terminals accept it, but batteries and signal fail, so don't rely on it alone. A day of paying, in order Land, and take a modest amount of crowns out of a bank ATM. Buy a transport ticket in the PID app before you board. Pay for breakfast and lunch by tapping. Keep a few coins for the toilet at the station. In the evening, a pub tab is settled at the table and the tip is easiest in cash. Nothing in that day needs a currency exchange booth. If your card is declined for no obvious reason, the likely cause is your own bank's fraud check on an unfamiliar country. Tell your bank before you travel, and keep its phone number somewhere other than your phone. Is it safe to use my card in Prague? As safe as in most European cities. Keep the card in sight when you pay, cover the PIN pad and check the amount on the terminal before you tap. If a card goes missing, call your bank at once, and keep its emergency number somewhere other than your phone. What if I run out of cash on a Sunday? Banks are closed on Sundays, but ATMs aren't. Many shops in the centre open on Sundays, and supermarkets, pharmacies and petrol stations take cards. Small things Prices in shops and on menus are shown in crowns and include value-added tax. A service charge, if there is one, should be stated on the menu. Shops are required to give you a receipt, so expect one. Frequently asked questions Can I pay in euros in Prague? Some tourist shops take euros, but the rate is poor and change comes back in crowns. A card or crowns are almost always better. Which ATM should I use? One attached to a bank branch. Free-standing machines on tourist streets can charge higher fees and offer weak exchange rates. Should I choose CZK or my home currency at the terminal? Choose CZK. The home-currency option mainly suits the merchant, and its rate is generally worse than your own bank's. Do I need cash for the toilet? Often, yes. Public toilets in stations and elsewhere frequently want coins. Before you fly, tell your bank you are travelling, load a wallet app and pack a handful of coins. Everything else you can fix on arrival.
